#311. The 10 best hookup apps of 2026: I swiped until my thumb hurt

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Thanks to hookup apps like Tinder and Pure, we can get “dates” (and I use that term loosely) with the tap of a button. Finding a sexy new friend can be as straightforward as ordering a pizza. As for the quality? That’s about the same as your pizza — hit or miss, depending on the time of day, where you’re located, and how hungry you are.

I’ve spent the past four years (yes, years) testing dozens of the top dating apps for Mashable, from discreet sexting apps to dating sites for serious relationships. My goal is simple: to find the best apps for every kind of dater, including the one-night-stand crowd. I also consulted sex and relationship experts about being upfront, setting boundaries, and taking things offline.

Tinder is my top pick for most people looking for a hookup. If you’d rather keep your real name off your profile and be direct about your turn-ons, try Pure. Feeld is where I’d start for kink, non-monogamy, and exploring your sexuality. For queer men, I’d start with Grindr, or Sniffies if you’re specifically interested in cruising. HER is my pick for queer women. Hinge is worth considering for an ongoing casual connection, but be upfront: Plenty of people there want a relationship. The best hookup apps, reviewed by our experts AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections Tinder — top pick for fast hookups Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups Pure — best for anonymous hookups OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups

Pure — best for anonymous hookups

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity

You don’t have to pretend you’re looking for a relationship to get a date. If you want a one-night stand or a regular FWB, say so.

"Hookup apps help prevent situations where people are on mainstream dating sites with the intention of having a casual hookup but are unclear about these intentions," Suzannah Weiss, sex/couples therapist and resident sexologist for Erojoy, tells Mashable. "They also give women a space to be openly sexual creatures without judgment."

Once you've matched, reach out, be honest, and follow through! "Plan dates within the first conversation or else you'll get tired out from having a bunch of conversations that aren't going anywhere," Weiss says.

As you may know, I've tested a lot of dating apps (like, a lot). But if someone asks me for the quickest way to find a hookup, I still tell them Tinder. CEO Spencer Rascoff is trying to move the app away from its "hookup reputation" to attract Gen Z and bring in more women, but that's probably not why you're here.

Either way, people are coming back. Tinder's daily active users grew year over year in September for the first time in three and a half years, per Match Group's third-quarter results. Tinder also says it's made over 100 billion connections worldwide since launch.

It's built for quick connections, not long love stories (though some people, including Mashable's Tech Editor, met their long-term partner on the app).

"Tinder, hands down, is the best app for hookups," Michelle Herzog, LMFT and AASECT-certified sex therapist, tells Mashable. "Over the past decade or so, it's morphed from being the early 20s hookup central to a place for adults of all ages to go for a quick one-nighter." Weiss adds that it's "probably the most popular hookup app among college students."

Tinder has added a lot of features that feel more relationship-y lately, like turning "Double Date" into "Modes" and launching its own reality show, Double Date Island. I still think it's the best app for casual flings. Its 2026 trend predictions even included "Clear-Coding," aka being upfront about what you want so nobody wastes their time. (Which, honestly, is my No. 1 rule for hookup apps.)

If you'd feel better with your friends there, try Group Hangouts. It launched in the U.S. on Sept. 30 and started rolling out in the U.K. on Nov. 23. You and at least two friends pick an activity and "like" other groups. If at least one person from each group likes the other, everyone ends up in a group chat to make plans. Double Date works the same way, just with you and one friend.

There's also the "Events" tab, where you can RSVP to low-key hangouts like bar trivia or Chinatown mahjong. It expanded to London, Manchester, and Birmingham in November, and about 30 percent of events are free. Tinder is also testing an AI-powered "Missed Connections" feature in Canada and Australia that shows you a weekly list of people you've physically crossed paths with. I'm super curious whether that one makes it to the U.S.

Of course, there's AI, too, including a "Chemistry" matchmaker and an algorithm that prioritizes "Sparks" (real back-and-forth conversations). I'd still take the algorithm's suggestions with a grain of salt. "Algorithmic curation, at its current level of sophistication, is very good at showing you more of what you've already responded to and significantly less good at showing you what could work better," says Caroline Millet, a dating burnout coach and former matchmaker. "If your 'type' is so good, why are you still looking?" One thing AI can't do is talk for you: Rascoff says AI agents are banned on Tinder and Hinge.

On the safety side, Tinder now requires new members to scan their face (Face Check) before they can join. It started in California in October 2025 and has expanded since. It's not perfect. Scammers have found workarounds, and an October Senate report found that, as of late 2025, Tinder hadn't updated most of its AI scam detection models in years. (Match added a new one this year.) Match Group says Face Check and its other safety updates have cut exposure to potential bad actors by more than 60 percent, and it invests $125 million a year in trust and safety. My advice? If your match gets weird about their photos or wants to move to WhatsApp right away, unmatch.

Read our full review of AdultFriendFinder.

Pure is for the adventurous dater (with a growing Gen Z and millennial fan club) who is so over the mainstream options and the endless stream of low-effort "heys." If you want an uncomplicated, no-strings-attached hookup where you can be direct about your desires without judgment, this is the app. It's unconventional, artsy, and built for anonymity. In my experience, it's also the exact place to be for steamy conversations or super-hot phone sex with a stranger. Plus, Pure says its users are split 60/40 between men and women — a surprisingly balanced ratio.

I picked Pure because it's "hot, weird, and way better than Bumble" for making casual connections. Its best features are designed for direct, exciting encounters: chats disappear after 24 hours unless you both agree to keep them, and you don't have to put your real name on your profile.

In my four weeks of testing this anonymous hookup app, I was honestly surprised by the results. The conversations were leagues above what I've found on other apps, and I received hundreds of likes daily, even outside of a major city like New York. While anonymity can be a concern, Pure balances it with safety features like Photo Verification and a "True Photo" request, which lets you ask for a live photo in your chat to confirm you're talking to a real person.

To combat the "app fatigue," Pure rolled out a major feed redesign in April. You'll now see one profile at a time, making the experience feel much more intentional. The company also added new "Profile Aesthetics" so you can customize your ad with loud color patterns (like bright pink or periwinkle). Bonus: Your "Turn-ons" are now front and center, and a new "Mutual Turn-Ons" view instantly highlights the kinks and interests you share with a potential match before you even say hello.

Pure is also getting serious about safety. In December 2025, the app launched "Safety Signal," a feature that lets you share your location and date details with a trusted contact when you take things offline. In August 2026, Pure added "My Media Rules," a digital bouncer that lets you set universal boundaries to auto-block all incoming nudes, turn off media sharing, or adjust photo permissions on a chat-by-chat basis. In the UK, Pure also requires age verification before users can post their first ad.

"Consent should not begin when two people meet in person. It begins with how someone communicates, what they send and whether they respect a boundary the first time," says Sandra Hatton, a professional matchmaker and founder of When We First. "Technology can create another layer of protection, but it should support consent, not replace the responsibility of users to behave respectfully."

That said, it's a space to navigate with intention. Anonymity is the whole point of Pure, but it shouldn't mean flying blind. "Anonymous should never mean untraceable to YOU," says Erica Arrechea, founder and CEO of Cinqe Matchmaking. "Before meeting someone, know who you're actually meeting. Meet publicly first!"

Pure doesn't have built-in background checks, so I'd look for the Photo Verification badge and send a True Photo request before you meet. (Here's how to vet your Pure matches.)

Weiss also notes that Pure isn't as specifically geared toward the kink and queer communities as Feeld, so you may encounter more straight cis men who are just looking for a conquest. The biggest trade-off is its smaller user base compared to mainstream apps like Tinder, though its recent 95 percent year-over-year registration growth and new status as a top-8 grossing lifestyle app in the U.S., UK, and France show it's rapidly closing the gap.

I know, I know: Hinge is supposedly "designed to be deleted." But honestly, I think it's one of the best apps for finding a regular hookup, especially if you like a little connection first. If you live in a reasonably populated area and Tinder gives you the ick, Hinge is a really good alternative.

Just know that plenty of people on Hinge want a relationship, so please be upfront about wanting something casual. I like it best for finding a regular FWB. If you want someone to come over tonight, I'd try a different app.

Hinge's "Dating Intentions" section lets you say exactly what you're looking for, and according to the app, 75 percent of Gen Z daters check it before sending a "like." So if you want something short-term, say so. It saves everyone time.

And don't stress too much about your opener. In Hinge's October flirting report, 65 percent of Gen Z daters said they'd rather someone flirt a little awkwardly but make their interest obvious than be smooth and leave them guessing. (Same, honestly.)

I also love that Hinge lets free users see everyone who "likes" them (one at a time). Most apps blur those photos until you pay. (Looking at you, eharmony.) You get eight free "likes" a day and can chat with matches for free. Hinge also picks out "Standouts" (profiles the algorithm thinks are your best potential matches), but you need a "Rose" to like them, and you only get one free Rose a week.

If you want more filters but don't want to pay for Hinge+ or HingeX, there might be another option soon. Hinge is testing a cheaper subscription tier with extra filters and custom location boundaries, and it's supposed to launch by the end of 2026.

When you're ready to meet up, "Date Ideas" lets you add three date options to your profile, like grabbing drinks or seeing live music. Matches can pick an idea and a time before they send a "like," so you can skip the "we should hang out sometime" back-and-forth.

In June, Hinge also launched its "Signals" badge. The purple heart shows up on verified users who've recently been "Thoughtful Participants," like messaging their matches and confirming dates. It's helpful, but it doesn't guarantee someone won't flake. "Treat app features as additional information, not proof of intention," says Hatton. "A badge or longer response window can be helpful, but seriousness ultimately shows up through behavior."

If you get stuck on what to say, Hinge's AI-powered "Convo Starters" feature suggests icebreakers based on someone's profile. I'd keep AI away from your photos, though. Hinge says 88 percent of its daters are uncomfortable with AI-generated profile pictures.

Hinge also now requires new users to complete "Face Check," a video-selfie scan, in a growing number of regions. Hinge says the scan doesn't guarantee someone's identity or safety, though. On Oct. 1, it also announced a new approach to minor harassment: Human moderators can issue a warning and require an educational walkthrough before someone can use the app again.

If you're a woman or non-binary person who wants something casual without a flood of creepy messages, Bumble is where I'd start. Yes, it ended its famous "women message first" rule in August. But it's still way more structured than Tinder: Anyone can send one opening message, and the chat stays locked until the other person replies.

"Bumble is a helpful app for women who want to avoid being creeped on and only hear from men they're interested in," Weiss tells Mashable. And if you want someone who's upfront about wanting "fun, casual dates" or "intimacy, without commitment," you can find them here, too.

Whoever gets that opening message now has 72 hours to reply, up from 24, which takes a lot of pressure off. The change came straight from users, too. In a Bumble survey, 66 percent of women said they actually prefer men to send the first message.

That said, guys, please don't waste your one message on "hey girl." "Read her profile and talk to her like a human being," says Arrechea. "Not 'hey.' Not a copy-and-pasted pickup line."

Bumble also has an AI assistant called "Bee," but founder Whitney Wolfe Herd said on the company's August earnings call that it won't replace swiping. "Let me be clear: Bee is not replacing the swipe. We are not aiming for an AI-driven experience. Bee is simply the intelligence under the hood," she said. She also said bigger profile and IRL updates were coming in early 2027. In the meantime, Bumble added profile badges for "ethical non-monogamy" and "intimacy without commitment," so it's easier to say what you want.

Bumble is trying to get you offline faster. It's testing a "Suggest a Date" feature in Canada so you can skip the endless back-and-forth. In October, it launched "Handles," so you can give someone your @ instead of your phone number. (I love this for when you meet someone cute but aren't ready to hand over your number.) The optional feature is available to verified U.S. iOS users. Someone needs your exact handle to find you, and you still have to like each other before you can chat.

If one-on-one dates aren't your thing, Bumble also launched "Plans," a standalone app for meeting people IRL in small groups. It's open to anyone 21+, but only in New York City for now. There's also the "Instant Match" QR code, which lets you match with someone you meet at a bar and check whether they're verified before you go home with them.

I do want to be upfront about Bumble's issues, though. A class-action lawsuit alleges that Bumble failed to protect user data during a "massive" breach by the hacker group ShinyHunters earlier this year. And in October, Bumble announced a $1.3 billion deal to go private. Ithaca Holdings is taking over, and Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman are expected to become co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd is expected to become a strategic adviser and join the board of Bumble's new parent company, according to a Nov. 20 SEC filing. I'm not sure yet how any of this will change the app.

Even with all that going on, Bumble's free version is pretty solid. You can chat by text, voice, or video without paying, and free users get basic filters like age, distance, and verified profiles. Premium features (Bumble Boost or a premium membership) get you advanced filters, but you don't need them to find a hookup buddy.

Feeld is for the explorers: the singles, couples, and polycules looking to ethically explore non-monogamy, kink, and alternative relationship styles. If you find the binary options on most dating apps to be limiting, Feeld's inclusive, consent-forward environment is refreshing. It’s a hub for people practicing "relationship anarchy" or just curious about connections without traditional rules.

It's worth noting, however, that the app is attracting more "vanilla" users (those with conventional tastes) lately, which is changing the dynamic somewhat. But even those "normies" might be hiding a wild side: Feeld's "State of Reflections Volume 1: Am I Normal?" report found that 42 percent of mainstream, non-Feeld daters actually practice kink. And the community is getting more curious by the day.

Being sexually open-minded doesn’t mean you want to skip the buildup. Feeld’s latest “State of Dating” report surveyed 3,310 adults in the U.S. and UK and found that eight in 10 considered anticipation "crucial" to erotic excitement. And 58 percent said authenticity and clear intentions were missing from modern dating. You can want something casual and still want a little sexual tension before someone asks for your address.

Feeld has had its share of bugs, especially after its 2023 relaunch, and some users still report glitches. But nothing else does what it does for the kink community. And even as it gets more mainstream (Forbes reported in October that its revenue rose more than 30 percent in 2025), it's still one of the most sex-positive apps I've used.

The free “Constellation” feature lets you be transparent by linking your profile with up to five partners, and you can use more than 20 labels to define those connections, from "Lover" and "Dom" to "Friend with benefits." (While this feature links your profiles, your private chat histories and existing connections are not shared with your partners.) The app also offers detailed desire and kink tags, from "Bondage" to "Cuddling," so you can find exactly what you're looking for.

Feeld is also rolling out "Expiring connections." If neither of you sends a message within five days of connecting, you'll automatically disconnect, and that person goes back into your Discover feed. I like this one, since it pushes you to say hi before your connections pile up.

"Feeld is a good app for finding hookups because the people on it are sexually open-minded but also conscious," says Weiss. "Many of them are looking for casual sexual encounters, but not 'casual' in the sense of wanting to make a conquest or put in minimal effort," she adds. "I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date, as well as singles who want to explore different sexual fantasies and subcultures."

To make articulating those desires even easier, Feeld launched an interactive quiz called "Reflections" that helps you map out your boundaries, relationships, and kink affinities. And according to Feeld’s May 2026 “State of Reflections Volume 2: The Words We Didn’t Have” report, the quiz helped users put those desires into words. After taking the quiz, 72 percent of users said they changed (or thought about changing) how they communicate their desires on their profiles, and over half felt more empowered to bring up boundaries and safe sex right from the start. Once you finish the quiz, you get a custom link and QR code to share your dealbreakers with potential partners before you even meet.

If you're still figuring out how to put your relationship structure into words, Weiss suggests keeping it playful: "You can write something cute like 'ethical slut' or 'I have room for more than one love of my life in my heart' instead of just using the technical language."

If you're tired of Tinder, HUD is worth the download, and its tagline is literally "Fun without strings attached." HUD stands for "Honest, Upfront, and Direct," and it's the app for people who aren’t afraid to be their most authentic selves. Translation: If you're into non-monogamy, this is where you'll find like-minded people.

The people on this app aren’t here to find their forever person, but friends with benefits is definitely on the table. You might also find kinksters, ethical non-monogamous folks, and people interested in exploring relationship styles that are a little outside the mainstream. With more than 19 million users worldwide as of 2026, HUD offers many opportunities for your next hookup.

If Hinge and Pure had a baby, it would be HUD. This app doesn’t beat around the bush, but it’s also artsy in presentation and has a kinky-fun community behind it.

Like Hinge, you can answer prompts (up to three), add photos (up to five), and note whether you’re into smoking, drinking, or drugs. There’s also a really cool "My Bedroom" feature that lets you choose three "desires" that you’re really into, three "desires" you’re "open" to, and three you’re definitely not into. Examples include "bondage," "butt stuff," and "golden showers." There are tons of "desires" to choose from, even if you’re not that kinky, so have fun with it.

Speaking of kinky, HUD published its 2026 Pleasure Census, a global culture report in partnership with Girls Get Off. The survey revealed that 80 percent of daters aren't having as much sex as they'd ideally like, and those who openly talk about what they want in bed are three times more likely to reach orgasm with a partner every time. That's why features like "My Bedroom" are so great; they eliminate that awkward barrier to communication before you even meet up.

Besides "My Bedroom," HUD has an "Anti-Commitment Mode" badge you can add to your profile to let potential matches know why you're here. You’ll also get to pick your archetype (if you’re not sure what yours is, the app has a little quiz) to help you find your match. You can even add your favorite song to your profile.

Not sure how to explain that you're poly, kinky, or just not looking for anything serious? Keep it short. "You don't need to write a manifesto in your dating bio!" says Paulita Pappel, intimacy expert and founder of Lustery. "The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract."

The chat features are also a little more developed than those in a typical hookup app. You can engage with someone’s profile just by liking or commenting on their prompts, photos, etc. The video chat option also shows both cameras blurred until you both decide to reveal yourselves. Of course, you can get more features with a premium subscription, but the free version offers a lot.

Hily (short for "Hey, I Like You") is for anyone who wants a little more substance than Tinder's fast-swipe format but doesn't want to answer a ton of questions to get set up and start matching. The app gives you total flexibility: you can keep your profile simple, or fill out optional prompts, pick lifestyle passions, and take its 40-question "Icks&Clicks" compatibility quiz to see how compatible you are with potential matches before chatting.

Granted, my experience comes from living in a small Southern town (where more than 1,400 men were active at any given moment), but even compared to testing Hinge in the same spot, Hily brought out a distinct crowd. The user pool was packed with blue-collar guys, hunters, fishers, and dudes on motorcycles looking for low-pressure hangouts, casual flings, or sexting partners. While I didn't run into many queer women (mostly couples looking for a third), if you're looking for straight hookups with outdoorsy or country-leaning guys, the active user base makes finding a match easy.

Read our full review of the Hily dating app.

Even though it doesn't get as much attention as Tinder or Bumble, Hily has over 43 million users and lets you control how much effort you put into your profile. You can pick intentions like "Physical connection" or "Something casual," list up to 12 passions, and answer optional prompts under categories like "My Dating Guide" and "Life Vibes." It also features a "Roulette" wheel that hands out free daily perks like profile boosts and rollbacks.

There are a couple of quirks to keep in mind while browsing, though. While the "Finder" will show you people who match your set filters (like age, location, and gender), those preferences don't necessarily apply to who lands in your "Likes" feed. Plus, anyone who likes your profile stays blurred unless you pay for a subscription — unless you get lucky and win free "Unblurs" from the daily Roulette wheel or happen to stumble across them naturally in the "Finder."

If you're not too keen on receiving NSFW photos or chats, Hily added a feature called "Consent Guard." Built with sexologists, this tool scans incoming messages and photos for adult content and gives you a pop-up warning so you can decide whether you actually want to see a nude or explicit text before opening it. It keeps your inbox safe from surprise cyberflashing, but lets you turn up the heat as soon as you give the green light. "[Consent tools] make it less likely for users to be sexually harassed, while also allowing them to see who the culprits are so they can choose not to engage with them," says Weiss.

While other apps push AI matchmakers, Hily is taking a different approach. Its early 2026 "T.R.U.T.H. Report" showed that nearly 70 percent of daters feel AI matchmakers make dating feel fake. In response, Hily brought back its "HI" (Human Intelligence) campaign to focus on real human chemistry instead of automated matching algorithms.

If you're a gay, bi, trans, or queer man looking for a hookup, Grindr is still where most people start. There are other options out there, but nothing has more guys online at once. According to Grindr's "Unwrapped" report, users sent over 135 billion chats last year, and the most-searched profile tag was "Hung." (Of course it was.)

The free version isn't perfect, though. In his review, Tyler Schoeber said it's "overrun with intrusive ads," and it limits you to about 87 messageable profiles on the grid unless you upgrade. A Grindr XTRA membership can get pricey, too. The good news is that Grindr's 2026 roadmap includes "rewarded ads," which would let free users unlock premium features by watching an ad.

Even with the ads, Grindr is still the go-to hookup app for gay men because so many people use it.

Grindr's location-based grid makes it really easy to see who's nearby and available, which matters even more in smaller towns where the queer community might be limited. This year, Grindr is putting its "Right Now" feature directly on the map, so you can see who's looking to hook up near you. According to Grindr's data from May, Right Now is most popular in places like Taiwan, the Philippines, Lima, Buenos Aires, and Medellín. There's also "Discreet Posting," which lets you post a hookup request without showing your profile until you approve a chat.

Aside from getting your biscuit buttered, Grindr has become a hub for travelers. In May, it released the third season of its Host or Travel series, and its "Roam" feature lets you drop a pin anywhere in the world to see who's around before you even get there. Grindr's map is also being updated to show gay bars, clubs, and gyms, and the app is testing direct hotel bookings.

That said, Grindr has added a lot of safety features lately. Last year, it publicly supported the "App Store Accountability Act," which would have Apple or Google handle age verification at the device level, so you don't have to upload your ID to every app. It also added an in-app Safety Center and a "Taken on Grindr" timestamp that shows how recent someone's photos are. And through its Grindr for Equality initiative, it rolled out sexual health features like automated HIV testing reminders, status sharing, and PrEP and DoxyPEP profile options.

On Nov. 2, Grindr also finished acquiring Freddie, an online healthcare service that specializes in HIV prevention. If you're in the U.S. or Canada, you can use Freddie through Grindr's Health section to talk to a clinician, get tested, and get PrEP (medication that helps prevent HIV) delivered discreetly.

The ads are annoying, and the paid tiers add up fast. But for quick, location-based hookups, Grindr is still king.

HER was created by and for queer women, so you can meet women and nonbinary folks without worrying about "skeevy guys" sexualizing you. It launched in 2015, and while it isn't built just for hookups, it's a great place to find something casual (or something more, if that's what happens). It also has more than 15 million users, so there are plenty of people to meet.

From my own experience, HER still works. I met a really sweet girl in Nashville on HER, and we went on a few dates. So for now, it's still my top recommendation for queer women.

HER makes it easy to say what you want. The "Looking for" section on your profile lets you add a "something casual" tag that everyone can see. HER also added "Feelings," temporary tags like "Hook up" or "Flirty" that you can add to your profile to show what you're in the mood for right now.

The app works a lot like a social media platform. There's a social feed, events, and media for the LGBTQ+ community. The interface can feel a little clunky at first, but it's not hard to figure out. For safety, HER offers photo verification, so verified profiles get a checkmark badge.

In 2025, Match Group bought HER, and a lot of users weren't happy about it. Many people on Reddit worried it would lead to the "enshittification" of another queer platform they love. HER founder Robyn Exton said she was optimistic, and Match Group CEO Spencer Rascoff promised to "protect" what makes the app special. Now we're all just waiting to see if they actually do.

So far, the app's main features haven't really changed. HER started the year with a "Sapphic Restart" campaign about putting its community first. And it hasn't gotten any less horny, either. Its "Everything Reminds Me of HER" billboards in New York and Los Angeles were full of sexy innuendos, like champagne pouring over skin and fingers slipping into a bowling ball. They went viral on TikTok and Instagram because, of course, they did.

Sniffies is a web-based cruising platform built for one thing: finding sex, right now, with minimal small talk. Sniffies was deemed too hardcore for the App Store, and so it's not technically an app. It's a hookup destination for men seeking men who want spontaneous and anonymous encounters.

If you feel like Tinder and Grindr aren't direct enough, I'd like to introduce you to Sniffies, the hookup platform that brings cruising into the 21st century. It launched an official iOS app in March 2025, only to be kicked out of the App Store by May for being, well, too horny for Apple. But if you downloaded the app before it was removed, and haven't deleted it, it should still work.

As soon as you enter the website, you'll see a map of guys nearby who are looking for action in your area. (You don't have to deal with registering for an account or anything — pull up the site, choose to browse anonymously, complete the age verification and captcha, and you're in.) The "Cruiser Filters" let you search for exactly what you're into, from body type to endowment size to your favorite sex positions.

In April, Sniffies added a few updates to make finding someone even faster. "Cruiser Cards" is a scrollable carousel that highlights active guys nearby so you don't have to hunt around the map. They’ve also added a new "Into Filter" and "Position Icons" that put a cruiser’s intent and favorite sex positions directly on their map avatar.

When you're ready to meet, you can use the new "Share a Spot" feature to drop a temporary, expiring map pin directly into the chat. It’s much better than sending vague directions or swapping apps to share your location. They even added "Share a Group," which lets you send live group event details — like the time and who’s attending. And if you're planning a trip, "Travel Mode" lets you cruise another neighborhood or city before you get there. It's a Sniffies PLUS feature.

The app now has around three million monthly active users who send 20 million messages daily, and has even caught Match Group's attention. The company invested $100 million in Sniffies in April, a deal that also gives Match an option to buy the platform outright. On a November earnings call, Match Group CEO Spencer Rascoff said the company now owns "about half" of Sniffies.

If your idea of a perfect match is someone who can talk about the nuances of rope suspension one minute and be Dungeon Master for your next D&D night the next, you should probably be on FetLife. Just know that FetLife is a social network for the kink community, not a typical hookup app, so people might not appreciate it if you treat it like a swiping app. Still, it's the place online for established kinksters, which makes it great for meeting sexy new friends who share your very specific interests.

It's also my go-to for gamers. There isn't a hookup app made just for gamers that I'd recommend, but FetLife has a lot of self-described nerds, and there's a surprising amount of overlap between the gaming and kink communities.

"FetLife is popular among gamers and even has some subgroups specifically for kinky gamers," says Weiss. "The app/site tends to attract nerds and other fringe communities."

If you're nervous about making the first move, there's "Crushing On," which FetLife added in April. You can privately mark that you have a crush on someone, and they won't be notified. If they mark you too, FetLife lets you both know at the same time, so you can start a conversation from there.

Hily (added August 2026): I’ve added Hily to our top picks because its free tier is surprisingly generous (up to 100 likes a day!) and its AI safety tech (like Consent Guard) makes it a standout option for casual, blunt daters looking for a fresh alternative to the Big Three.

You might notice a few apps that pop up in ads or other lists are missing here. That’s intentional. I swipe through the good, the bad, and the downright sketchy so you don’t have to. For an app to make my list, it has to offer more than a convincing ad.

Here's a shortlist of apps that didn't make the cut:

Plenty of Fish: POF's rebrand didn't do it any favors. My last round of testing showed it removed key features like free messaging with non-matches, and I kept running into the same old profiles. (Removed January 2025.)

Match: Some people swear they've found casual hookups on Match, but that's not what it's for. It's still one of my top picks for a long-term relationship. For a hookup? You're fishing in the wrong pond. (Removed August 2025.)

Wild: You’ve probably seen ads for this one. On paper, Wild sounds like the perfect casual dating app. In practice, the paywalls are aggressive, the distance filter doesn't work, and you have to pay for anything that's even remotely useful. Unless you're willing to spend serious cash upfront (and hope for the best), the experience feels more limited than with more generous free options like Tinder or Hily.

DOWN: This app (formerly "Bang With Friends") is known for its simple "Get Down" vs. "Get Date" feature. It sounds clever, but in reality, the experience is messy at best. Many users report feeling scammed by subscriptions that don't deliver matches, or finding that the few real people on there are... let's say "odd." It’s hard to recommend an app when the main user complaint is "Is anyone real?" Hard pass.

Facebook Dating: Yes, Facebook has a dating section, and it’s surprisingly massive (and completely free, which is huge). While it's a decent option for casual dating, the vibe tends to be a bit more "friends of friends" and "relationship-focused" than the anonymous, no-strings energy you get from apps like Pure or Feeld. (For Mashable's Chance Townsend, signing up was "the most uneventful dating experience" of his life.) It's also added an AI dating assistant and "Meet Cute," which sends you one surprise match a week. It's worth a shot if you're already on Facebook, but it didn't quite crack my top tier for no-strings-attached hookups specifically.

Tinder is still the best hookup app for most people. Pure is worth trying if you want a more discreet profile, while Feeld is where I’d go for kink or ethical non-monogamy. For queer men, there’s Grindr or Sniffies; for queer women, HER.

Tinder lets you match and chat for free, Hinge shows your incoming likes one at a time, and I got up to 100 "likes" a day on Hily’s free version.

Pure is the best anonymous hookup app. You don’t have to put your real name on your profile, and chats disappear after 24 hours unless you both agree to keep them.

Bumble is worth considering. Either person can send the first message, but they can’t keep sending messages unless the recipient replies. Pure is worth trying if you want to be direct about your turn-ons, while HER is my top pick for queer women.

Feeld is where I’d start. “I often recommend this app to couples who want to find a third person to play with or date,” says Weiss. Say whether you’re dating together or separately and what you’re hoping to find. If you’re new to non-monogamy, have the boundaries conversation with your partner before involving someone else.

No app can guarantee your safety. Look for tools that give you control over who can contact you, what they can send, and how much personal information they can see.

Photo or face verification: Tinder’s Face Check uses a video selfie to help check that someone matches their profile photos. Bumble also offers photo verification and lets you ask a match to verify their photos.

Nude filters: Pure’s My Media Rules and Hily's Consent Guard let you block or screen explicit content before opening it. Bumble’s Private Detector automatically blurs potentially explicit photos, so you can decide whether to view them.

Date sharing: Pure’s Safety Signal lets you share your last-known location and date details with a trusted friend. Tinder’s Share My Date and Bumble’s Share Date let you share plans, including who you’re meeting, where, and when.

Blocking and reporting: Never use an app that makes it hard to report bad behavior. Bumble, for example, lets you block and report someone from their profile or chat without telling them who reported them.

Meet in a public place first, get yourself there and home, and tell a friend where you’ll be. “Casual sex does not require casual safety,” says Hatton. “Do not give a stranger your home address simply because the intention of the connection is casual.” Weiss also recommends having a friend check in later that night or the next morning.

They pressure you to drink or host immediately.

They pressure you to move off the app before you’re comfortable.

Be honest and specific about what you want, like “Looking for a regular FWB” or your specific kinks if you’re on Feeld. You don’t need to spell out every detail. “The bio is there to open the right door, not to function as a legal contract,” says Pappel.

Sometimes, but try the free version first. If you keep running into limits on profiles, filters, or messages, an upgrade might be worth it. A short subscription can also make sense for a trip — that’s when Tyler Schoeber recommends paying in his Grindr XTRA review. If you’re not interested in anyone you’re seeing, I wouldn’t rush to pay.

Here’s what I look for when testing hookup apps, from what you can do for free to how much control you have over who can contact you.

Hands-on testing: I create profiles on every app or site in this guide, including browser-based options like Sniffies. I check how easy it is to find people who want something casual, which features are free, and what’s locked behind a subscription.

Expert and community feedback: User reviews and Reddit threads help me compare my experience with other people’s. I also consulted the following experts about communicating intentions, setting boundaries, and meeting offline:

#310. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#309. Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years

Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.

The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about."

Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig said the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game launches and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

"We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more new customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig said. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year."

Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

Revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

#307. FIFA says a cyberattack against it targeted a 'limited set of personal and business information'

World football's governing body says the cyberattack targeted personal and business information. They struck at a sensitive time for the under-fire organization and its president, Gianni Infantino.

FIFA told news agencies on Thursday that it had been targeted by a person or group seeking access to its data.

"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency, issuing similar comments to other outlets.

Reuters cited a person "with direct knowledge of the matter" as saying that less than 0.1% of FIFA's total data had been compromised.

This person also said that no files from the controversial, abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project that looked to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors had been accessed.

FIFA said that it was working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement, in the aftermath of the event.

It did not say when the attack took place, list the precise nature of the compromised data or specify how unauthorized access to FIFA data had been sought, amid reports of people having posed as FIFA officials rather than actually hacking the organization or otherwise compromising its cybersecurity systems.

Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot of what it said were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the cyberattack when responding to a post saying that more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been posted.

FIFA did not explicitly state whether it was talking about the same supposed incident.

The breach comes at a sensitive time for the organization. Still reeling from the scandal following this summer's World Cup of its now-aborted plans to sell off World Cup commercial rights shares, it's now trying to secure another term for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.

Infantino is the favorite for an election on March 18, when he is expected toface challenges from Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France. But until the turbulence of the last six months, it seemed most likely he would simply stand unopposed and extend his 11-year tenure without a fight.

#306. I Found the Best Black Friday Streaming Deals (2026): Apple TV, Disney, HBO Max

Black Friday streaming deals are some of the only “free money” hacks in all of shopping, and they are one of my favorite things to highlight during this shopping bonanza. Sure, that brand-new TV you've been eyeing looks nice, but have you considered shaving 50 percent off that streaming subscription you've been wanting to sign up for?

Most of the biggest streaming services are offering Black Friday deals this year, as they do every year. Nearly all of these deals are for new and former customers only. #304. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#303. Freigang banned — Germany star to miss 2027 World Cup

Germany forward Laura Freigang has been suspended until October 2027 after missing three doping tests, ruling her out of next year's Women's World Cup in Brazil. Freigang has denied any intention to evade controls.

Laura Freigang is set to miss next year's women's World Cup in Brazil after being suspended for missing doping tests, the German Football Association (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday.

Freigang, who has played 45 matches for Germany and scored 17 goals, will be suspended until October 7, 2027 after reaching a settlement with the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency. The suspension is for the next 16 months as it began retroactively on June 8, 2026, when she was notified by the DFB, and prohibits Freigang from playing for club or country.

"It's important to me to emphasize once again that I was never suspected of doping," Freigang said in a statement on Instagram.

"My agreement to a settlement does not mean that I share all the assessments of my case. The past few months have been extremely difficult for me. Another legal process would have entailed significant financial, mental, and emotional strain. This is why I decided to take this path, in the hope of finding some peace, clarity and perspective for myself," she added.

"It was never my intention to let it get this far. Sports have defined my life since I was little. It breaks my heart that, for now, I won't be able to step onto the field, help my team, or live the daily life that I love so much."

This brings to a close a case that has been ongoing for months. The 28-year-old had been accused of not being where she said she would be for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.

In June, Freigang explained missing the tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis."

The ban ends her World Cup hopes, something the DFB has also acknowledged.

"We are simply so sorry for Laura on a personal level because of this situation. The past few weeks have been very stressful for her," said DFB Sporting Director Nia Künzer. "We hold her in high regard both as a player and as a person, and — as we have done in recent weeks — we will continue to stay in touch with her and support her as best we can."

The situation also puts her future at her club, Eintracht Frankfurt, into question. Freigang's contract runs until June next year.

"The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty through a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt — for us as a club, but above all for Laura," said Katharina Kiel, Frankfurt's director of women's football.

The club and Freigang, who has played 180 Bundesliga games in her career, are now set to enter talks to determine the shape of her contract moving forward.

Pretty much everyone: The iPad Air is not just the best iPad, it's the best tablet. It will be your new go-to device for streaming, reading, or creative projects. It's fast, moves smoothly between apps thanks to the M4 chip with 12GB of RAM, and has a stunning high-definition display.

Creatives on a budget: While we prefer the iPad Pro for creatives, the iPad Air is a more budget-friendly option that still handles tough design jobs. And if you plan on using your tablet as a substitute for a laptop, it'll work for that, too, especially when paired with the Magic Keyboard for iPad Air or Apple Pencil Pro. Both are sold separately, but add useful versatility to the tablet, essentially transforming it into a full workstation.

To kick off 2026, Apple upgraded the iPad Air to include the M4 chip. While the update didn't feel necessary in light of the already powerful iPad with M3 chip, we'll never say no to more computing power, especially with no price increase.

The iPad Air bridges the gap between tablet and laptop, yet it still remains affordable and user-friendly. With the M4 chip upgrade, the iPad Air got a performance boost, now scoring 13,176 on the Geekbench 6 test, up from its previous score of 11,464.

While the iPad Pro is technically slightly thinner and lighter, the iPad Air still lives up to its name. It's a great tablet to bring on the go due to its light weight, which helps avoid wrist strain when holding the device.

It has a crisp display for brilliant graphics, and one of its most surprising upgrades in the 2026 model is more memory. Now with 12GB of RAM, it's better equipped as a gaming device, too. For creatives too, the extra memory makes it even more capable of creative tasks, whether that be in Final Cut Pro or while doing design work with the Apple Pencil.

When we first published this guide, the iPad Air cost just $599. In the face of the global memory crisis, it has increased to $749. While this does impact its overall value, considering most other tech prices are on the rise, it's still well-positioned in the market.

Read our full review of the iPad Mini OLED.

Casual users: Our tech editor recently reviewed the new iPad Mini and had this to say: It's a darn near perfect tablet, except for the price. The newest Apple tablet has an 8.5-inch OLED display and is a mere 5.4mm thick, and it feels great in your hands. The new OLED display is fantastic, with incredible clarity, brightness, color, and contrast, even in direct sunlight. If you primarily use a tablet for gaming, scrolling, and watching TV shows and movies, this is the best iPad for you — if you can afford it.

The $699 retail price is asking a lot, but this tablet got a $100 price cut for Black Friday 2026. At $599, it's a lot easier to recommend.

The newest Apple tablet is a bit of an odd duck. Traditionally, the iPad Mini was a more affordable tablet, but with a premium OLED display and $699 price, it costs almost as much as the M4-powered iPad Air, which has a larger display. As a result, it occupies kind of a weird place in Apple's iPad lineup.

But if you want something more powerful than the base iPad and can afford to pay more for a higher-quality display, then we think you'll love the iPad Mini OLED.

Android users or those who want to branch out: Looking for an Android tablet? Our pick is the Lenovo Yoga Tab. It's an exceptional value that performs on par with Apple's iPads. It's a fast-moving tablet, delivering laptop-quality speeds, and almost feels like one with the included keyboard and pen.

Note takers: If you think you need an iPad for writing and drawing on a tablet, think again. The Lenovo Yoga Tab is the best writing experience on any tablet we've tested.

Right off the bat, I liked the Lenovo Yoga Tab. Setting it up is a breeze, and the apps downloaded quickly. After an initial charge, the Lenovo Yoga Tab's battery life lasted nearly an entire week when I used it a couple of hours per day.

Its performance was undeniable, and the Geekbench 6 confirmed that. The Lenovo Yoga Tab's multi-core score was 5,799, on par with the iPad's 6,233 score and nearly double the OnePlus Pad Go 2's 3,030 score.

What I like best about the Lenovo writing experience is the haptic feedback. While the screen is smooth and glossy like any tablet, the pen has a roughed tip that makes it feel like an actual pen on paper. It's easily the best writing experience I've had on a tablet, and that's not to mention Lenovo's built-in note-taking app has a better user interface than both Apple and Samsung.

Each Yoga Tab includes a keyboard case and pen, so you're getting more than just a tablet. On Lenovo's site, it's given an estimated value of $619.99, but I've never seen it priced higher than $419.99. That's an amazing deal, considering an iPad with equivalent accessories will run you $677.

I should say, I don't love the case on the Lenovo Yoga Tab, finding it stiff and not the most well-balanced. The keyboard and stylus, though, are far superior in design.

You're done with Amazon's Fire tablets: If you've used Fire tablets for years but want something with serious performance then you need to go for Amazon's Alexa tablets. The 12 Pro is an elite model and an Amazon tablet that can actually compete with Apple iPads. It's a tablet that you can work on, especially when used with the Alexa Tablet Pro Keyboard.

Amazon Fire tablets have never been our favorites. That's why the new Amazon Alexa tablets were a welcome upgrade. The Amazon Alexa 12 Pro is an excellent tablet with an upgraded processor. It finally has access to the Google Play Store, meaning no longer are you stuck with the Amazon app store.

I was chocked at how powerful it was with a Geekbench score of 6,498, which is better than the iPad with A16 chip and on par with the Samsung Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra. However, it's a far better value than the S11 Ultra as it's only $679.99 compared to the S11 Ultra's price of $1,499.99. Plus, it's battery life is unreal. After running it for 12 hours, it still had 43% of its battery left.

Even artists can enjoy the 12 Pro as the nanomatte display keeps it glare free and adds some nice traction when using the included stylus.

iOS users on a budget: If you prefer saving money over splurging on the latest tech, the Apple iPad (11th generation) gets the job done. It's the base model, meaning it won't have the fastest processor like the iPad Air's M4 chip or the latest features like Apple Intelligence. However, it is the most affordable Apple tablet, even with its price increase to $449.

Kids: Plus, it's especially great for kids if you want to get them a tablet but don't want to spend a fortune on it.

Most of Apple's iPads now have the M-series of chips; however, the classic iPad has the A-series, typically found in iPhones. That being said, the 11th-generation iPad still offers enough processing power for everyday use thanks to its A16 Bionic chip. You'll be able to multitask without the system sputtering out, whether you're watching YouTube videos, playing your favorite high-res games, or just have a habit of leaving your apps running in the background. It also packs a decent amount of storage space. The base model starts at 128GB, so there's no need to pick and choose what apps and pictures you want to keep. Speaking of, it sports 12MP front and rear cameras with Center Stage, a feature that keeps you in frame during FaceTime calls.

Combine all these features with the functionality of iPadOS 26 (yes, the A16 iPad is compatible with iPadOS 26), and you have an iPad that looks unassuming but is anything but — and all for a pretty unbeatable price point. It's a fine choice if you're just dipping your toes into tablets; however, creative professionals might prefer the power of the iPad Air or Pro.

Even though its tech is basic compared to the advanced iPad Air and Pro, it's great for someone who wants a portable screen for streaming, playing games, and reading. It's also a nice choice if you're interested in using your tablet as a laptop, but don't want to spend a ton of money. It's compatible with the Magic Keyboard Folio and together costs $598 — the same price as the iPad Air.

Gamers who want a smaller screen: Looking for a tablet to game on? There aren't a ton of options, as most just tackle mobile games, but what about full video games with extensive graphics? For that, there's the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5, which is designed for gaming. With over 12 hours of battery life, impressive processing, and a designated gaming hub.

Lenovo makes tablets that compete with not just iPads but MacBooks, too. That's thanks to the Snapdragon chip at the heart of the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5. Having tested previous generations of the Lenovo Legion Tab, we have a soft spot for this lineup. It has a compact 8.8-inch screen, which makes it ultra portable and comfortable for handheld gaming, but I didn't expect this tablet to be so powerful.

On the Geekbench 6 test, the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 had a 3,655 single-core score and a 10,758 multi-core score. That single-core score puts it on par with MacBooks. Plus, the Gen 5's 10,758 multi-core score is a huge boost over the Gen 3's score of 6,674. It handles livestreams like a pro, playing clear high-resolution video without any buffering. Plus, with 12 hours and 24 minutes of battery life, it outlasts most gaming laptops. It's outfitted with two USB-C ports, too, so you can plug in a charger and a controller simultaneously.

My only concern with the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is its touchscreen, which occasionally had some response time issues. This is a larger issue for games utilizing touchscreen, but less of a concern if you're using a controller.

Read our full review of the iPad Pro (M5).

Professionals: Released in 2025, the new iPad Pro is loaded with Apple's fastest M5 chip, giving it way more power than the average user really needs. Most people won't need this much power, which is why the iPad Air is our top pick.

Photo and video editors: Graphic designers can store all of their creative work on the device, which has up to 2TB of storage. It's also a smart choice for video editors, though the premium nano-texture glass, which prevents glare while working in any environment, even full sun, will cost extra. Plus, the XDR Retina display lets you play back HDR video and use this tablet as a reference monitor. For creative professionals, the Apple iPad Pro is a dream come true. It's also compatible with the Apple Pencil Pro, a tool that features a unique squeezable design and a barrel roll feature, enhancing precision and control in design work.

While the iPad Air is going to be the best for most people, the iPad Pro levels things up for professionals.

The 2025 iPad Pro isn't just a great tablet but an outstanding laptop. Loaded with Apple's latest M5 processing chip, it's one of the most advanced options from Apple. When running the Geekbench 6 tests, it scored between 16,200 and 16,400. That puts it in the top 8 percent of all laptops we've tested. That's miraculous levels of power for such a sleek, razor-thin package.

You can often find 1TB of storage in computers, but 2TB is rare in a laptop and nearly unheard of with a tablet, so it can store large files without a problem.

Android users who want a professional tablet: If you're an Android user who's seeking out a tablet that is well-equipped to handle all the tasks of a laptop, let us point you in the direction of the Samsung Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra. It has a beautiful AMOLED screen that enhances contrast and color depth and the 120Hz refresh rates makes everything from scrolling to handwriting smoother. While we wish the MediaTex processor was stronger, it still handles multiple apps at a time, allowing you to split the screen between apps. It even comes with a stylus for illustration or note-taking.

The Samsung Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra is one of the largest tablets out there, with a 14.6-inch screen. The screen size admittedly feels overkill, making it difficult to use when you're just trying to watch a show or browse the internet. But on the upside, with that giant screen, you can use multiple apps at once, allowing you to watch and play games at the same time. However, reading on the S11 Ultra is difficult, simply because the device is just so oversized that it's hard to hold, and there's just too much screen size unless you shrink the window.

But it's built for much more than reading. It starts with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, but goes up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. The S11 Ultra tablet has a MediaTek Dimensity 9400+ processor and a Geekbench 6 multi-core score of 8,797. That makes it not quite as powerful as Apple's iPad Pro or Air, but the most powerful Android tablet we've tested. Not to mention it scores higher than the standard iPad's Geekbench 6 score.

Its battery life is extremely impressive. When conducting a battery rundown test, it lasted 16 hours and 6 minutes, potentially allowing you to work on it for two days before needing a charge.

The stylus comes included with the S11 Ultra, and it's a lightweight pencil with a button to control the settings with a simple click. It writes beautifully and allows for a lot of precision, though some might prefer something with a bit more heft behind it.

If you are going to do work on the device, I recommend getting a keyboard and cover that doubles as a stand. Since the tablet is just so large, it's awkward to hold and type on. The keyboard and stand, however, make it feel like a great laptop while still maintaining the convenience of a tablet.

You also need to think about what operating system you prefer. iOS is great to use, but if all your other devices are Android-based, you may prefer to stick with Android. A third option is to consider a ChromeOS-based tablet — but again, you probably want it to play nicely with other devices. Go with what you're comfortable with.

Tablets are a great middle-ground between laptops and smartphones. If you've ever felt like you need more real estate than your smartphone's screen to watch your favorite show, draw a design, or simply browse the internet, a good tablet means you don't have to worry about digging out your laptop. The best tablet blends the convenience of a laptop with the lightweight nature of a phone. Easy to toss into your bag and take traveling, they can entertain your kids or give you something to do while on the move, all without being as full-on as a PC.

If you buy an Apple iPad, you can use FaceTime to call friends and enjoy video chats with them. #301. Dark Matter Might Have Its Own Periodic Table of Invisible Particles

Dark matter accounts for approximately 85 percent of all matter in the universe, though that’s about all we really know about the mysterious substance. Scientists believe it because of the gravitational effects it has on galaxies and other cosmic structures, but since it doesn’t otherwise interact with ordinary matter, it’s been a challenge for scientists to determine what it’s really made of.

For decades, scientists have been trying to determine whether dark matter consists of a single type of particle or if it’s made up of several particles that could have different properties and thus different interactions with the surrounding world. Earlier this year, scientists found the most convincing evidence of a dark matter particle yet, and if the second scenario is true, it’s possible we could find more.

This second possibility also raises an intriguing question: If there are a variety of “dark particles,” could they interact and combine with one another—just as the particles we know do—to form their own dark atoms and molecules? If that were the case, the dark universe could be much more complex than researchers had initially imagined.

But luckily, humanity has already faced a similar challenge in trying to understand the diversity of ordinary matter. Though to many introductory chemistry students, the periodic table can seem like an odd way to organize information, it’s one of the most ingenious tools developed in our understanding of the physical world. This classification system doesn’t just order the elements, but reveals patterns among their properties that even helped predict the existence of other elements that had not yet been discovered.

Now, a team of five physicists is exploring a scenario in which dark matter could form different classes of nuclei and atoms, governed by their own rules. Their research suggests that we may need something similar to a periodic table to understand the organization of dark matter.

The hypothesis at the heart of this research seems straight out of science fiction. The researchers propose that our universe would contain a kind of “mirror sector,” where particles that barely interact with visible matter have their own forces and can interact with one another.

The idea is not new and is quite serious. The “Mirror Twin Higgs” was proposed two decades ago as a possible solution to a problem related to the mass of the Higgs boson. According to this theory, mirror particles would help offset certain quantum effects that might otherwise cause its mass to be much greater than what we observe. Although the existence of these particles has never been proven, the proposal offered an ingenious way to address the problem without requiring all new particles to be visible to detectors.

One of the creators of the Mirror Twin Higgs theory, physicist Zackaria Chacko, is part of this new investigation that extends this hypothesis into the dark matter puzzle. Along with several collaborators, he explores in this recent preprint what would happen if particles from this hypothetical mirror sector could combine with one another, forming nuclei, atoms, and a variety of dark elements.

Their calculations suggest that, under certain conditions, these particles could combine to form dark equivalents of some of the elements we know, ranging from the simplest to others as complex as carbon. However, this would not be an exact copy of our matter. The dark particles would have different masses and properties, which would also change the rules governing how they bond, what structures they can form, and which ones remain stable.

For example, in the researchers’ model, dark hydrogen atoms would be unstable and could not survive as those in our universe do. This is a striking difference when we consider that hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in ordinary matter.

If these dark elements were ever discovered, understanding the rules governing their formation would be essential for classifying them. A sort of “dark periodic table” could help bring order to that diversity, just as it did with the elements we know.

For now, this all remains in the realm of theoretical physics. Researchers have not observed any of these atoms, and some doubt such structures could actually form. But there’s plenty about dark matter we have yet to discover.

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
